text: When exact numbers matter more than shape, you reach for one of two visuals. Here's the more powerful one, and the one worth mastering first.

A matrix works like an Excel PivotTable — fields on rows and columns both, automatically aggregated at every intersection. Year and Quarter down the side, Subcategory and Product across the top, Units Sold filling every single cell where a row and a column meet. A plain table can't do any of that — it only handles one category per row, with no hierarchy at all.

Plus and minus icons on the headers let viewers drill into more detail or collapse back to a clean summary, one level at a time. Or turn on Auto expand under Row headers and Column headers options in the Format pane, so every level shows the moment the visual first loads — no clicking required from your audience at all.

And by default, row headers stay frozen in place as the matrix scrolls horizontally — category labels never disappear off screen, no matter how many columns you're comparing side by side. Turn that off under Layout, Freeze, if you'd rather headers scroll away with everything else. You can even hand viewers a custom total — average instead of sum, for instance — right from a column's context menu.
Next: the everyday comparison and trend visuals — bar, column, line, and pie charts, the ones you'll reach for constantly in almost every report you build.
